title: Yousef Makki: Boy, 17, cleared of stabbing teenager to death
summary:
A 17-year-old, known as Boy A, has been cleared of murdering Manchester Grammar School pupil Yousef Makki, also 17, whom he stabbed in the heart with a flick knife in Hale Barns, Greater Manchester, on 2 March. Boy A claimed self-defence and was also found not guilty of manslaughter after a four-week trial at Manchester Crown Court.

After the verdict, Yousef's father, Ghaleb Makki, banged on a Perspex divider, shouted at jurors ("Where's the justice for my son?") and collapsed in tears. The judge cleared the courtroom.

A second 17-year-old, Boy B, was cleared of perverting the course of justice and conspiracy to rob. Both were cleared of conspiracy to commit robbery.

The court heard the privileged teenagers led "double lives," playing at being middle-class gangsters, smoking cannabis and posting threatening videos. They planned to rob a drug dealer, but it went wrong. Later, Boy A and Yousef fought, and Boy A said both drew knives and Yousef was accidentally stabbed. The defendants hid the knives and lied to police. Both admitted possessing a knife, and Boy A pleaded guilty to perverting the course of justice. Sentencing is due on 25 July.

title: Whistleblowers: 'We spoke out and lost our jobs'
summary:
MPs and peers are calling for a radical overhaul of UK whistleblowing law, saying the Public Interest Disclosure Act (1998) is "no longer fit for purpose" because it is too complicated and leaves many people unprotected. The All Party Parliamentary Group for Whistleblowing gathered evidence from more than 400 people, covering cases such as child sex abuse, financial fraud, bullying and discrimination.

One of them, "Katherine" (not her real name), and her husband taught at a southern England boarding school for over twenty years. They lost their jobs after exposing what she calls "systematic exam malpractice," including teachers completing students' coursework and letting them alter papers after exams. She says she was discouraged from using the school's whistleblowing procedure, and the exam board told her only disclosures to Ofqual were legally protected. The couple signed non-disclosure agreements in exchange for compensation, as they had no income. The NDA asks her to waive whistleblowing rights. She describes feeling suicidal, and her family was split up.

Group chair Stephen Kerr wants an independent Office for the Whistleblower to investigate complaints, penalize wrongdoers and offer counselling, legal advice and job protection. The group also seeks a broader definition of whistleblowing and protection for groups such as volunteers, foster carers, clergy and army members.

title: YouTube users can't stop streaming Latin Pop
summary:
YouTube, which reaches over 1.9 billion people monthly, shows that global listening tastes are increasingly dominated by non-English music, especially Latin pop. South Korea's Blackpink hit 468 million views with *Kill This Love*, while BTS's *Boy With Luv* ranks eighth. India's Dhvani Bhanushali, signed to T-Series, had the first Indian track to reach 50 million views in seven days.

title: Russia mini-sub fire: Putin issues heroism awards
summary:
Russian President Vladimir Putin awarded top state honors to the 14 crew members who died during a secret submarine mission on 1 July. Four captains received Hero of Russia medals, two other officers already held that title, and the remaining ten officers received the Order of Courage. The Kremlin said the crew heroically contained a fire and kept it from reaching the nuclear power unit, but died from inhaling toxic smoke. Survivors brought the vessel back to Severomorsk, and the dead are being buried in St Petersburg.

The government refused to name the submersible or give mission details, citing secrecy, but says it should return to service soon. It was widely reported to be an AS-12 or AS-31 "Losharik." Tass said the officers were linked to the military's secret deep-water research directorate, GUGI. One of them, Denis Dolonsky, received his Hero medal for the 2012 Arktika mission, which collected Arctic seabed rock samples to support Russia's territorial claim.

Analyst Pavel Felgenhauer questioned why 14 sailors died of smoke inhalation despite oxygen masks and emergency supplies, why so many senior officers were aboard, and why a vessel capable of diving to 6,000m was used in the shallow Barents Sea. Russia is competing for Arctic resources.

title: Boris Johnson in 'deal or no deal' Brexit challenge to rival Hunt
summary:
Boris Johnson has urged his Conservative leadership rival Jeremy Hunt to commit to leaving the EU on 31 October "deal or no deal," calling it the "central question" of the contest to succeed Theresa May, with the result due on 23 July. In a Talk Radio interview and a letter tweeted to Mr Hunt, Mr Johnson said he would stick to the date "come what may, do or die," arguing that doing so is the only way to restore trust in democracy.

Mr Hunt, who also wants to renegotiate Mrs May's Withdrawal Agreement, particularly the Irish backstop, would back no deal only as a last resort. He has hinted he might seek extra time if close to a better deal, warning that a rigid deadline risks triggering a general election and "political suicide" for the Conservatives.

Mr Hunt suggested Mr Johnson fears debating the issue after Sky News scrapped a planned debate when Mr Johnson refused to attend. Mr Hunt's team accused him of "bottling it."

Mr Johnson has struggled to explain how he would secure a deal in time. He claimed a "new dynamic" and "goodwill" had emerged since the European elections, insisted the backstop must go despite EU rejections, and suggested he could "suspend" the £39bn divorce bill until securing trade and border commitments.

title: Contaminated blood inquiry: More witnesses prompt extension
summary:
The NHS infected blood inquiry is being extended because of the large number of witnesses coming forward. Chairman Sir Brian Langstaff said almost 3,000 people have submitted or promised statements. After hearings in London, Leeds, Belfast, Edinburgh and Cardiff, four extra days (29 October to 1 November) have been added when proceedings resume in London on 8 October.

Up to 30,000 people, many with haemophilia or other bleeding disorders, were infected with HIV and hepatitis viruses through contaminated blood in the 1970s and 80s, which has been called the NHS's biggest treatment disaster.

Sir Brian said evidence across the UK showed a "very consistent picture" of problems with consent, communication, delays in informing patients of diagnoses, poor treatment by others, and stigma. Some accounts were highly individual, including that of Cardiff brothers Haydn and Gareth Lewis, who died within seven months of each other. Emails showed a government-appointed support trust called Haydn, a campaigner, a "moaner" and "thick". The inquiry also heard how seven-year-old Colin Smith, who died in 1990, and his family suffered abuse and vandalism.

Sir Brian praised witnesses' courage but said the inquiry lacks "the luxury of time," noting someone dies of hepatitis C every four days.

title: Wireless electric car charging gets cash boost
summary:
The government is investing nearly £37m in electric vehicle charging infrastructure, even as plug-in hybrid sales fell sharply. The Department for Transport (DfT) says the money will support UK engineering and "transform" the charge point network, including wireless charging and "pop-up" pavement chargers.

Plug-in hybrid sales dropped 50.4% in June, from 4,571 to 2,268 vehicles, after the government scrapped its £2,500 grant. Battery electric car registrations rose 61.7% to 2,461, according to the SMMT. Overall, though, the alternatively fuelled vehicle sector shrank for the first time since April 2017. The government also cut the subsidy for pure electric cars from £4,500 to £3,500. It plans to end sales of new conventional petrol and diesel cars and vans by 2040. The DfT said it is "focusing on the cleanest, zero emission models."

Char.gy received £2.3m to develop wireless induction charging for residential streets, using a pad under the car that aligns with one beneath the road. Retrofitting a car costs about £1,000, but some pilot participants will get pads free. Urban Foresight was awarded £3m for pavement-embedded chargers to help drivers without off-street parking.

The funding marks the first anniversary of the Road to Zero strategy, which aims for almost every UK car and van to be zero emission by 2050.

title: Wales' Jewish history: Call to record it before it is too late
summary:
Volunteers from the Jewish History Association of South Wales (JHASW) are racing to record the 250-year history of Jews in the region before it is lost. A century ago Wales had about 6,000 Jewish people; today the number is in the hundreds, many aged 80 or over. Of 72 people interviewed since August 2017, seven have died, and the average age of the rest is 85.

The group has crowdfunded £3,000 toward a permanent archive. A touring exhibition currently displays 72 oral histories and 6,000 images, but placing the material online and in museums could cost £60,000. Organisers hope Heritage Lottery Fund money will cover this and help train volunteers to search museums and libraries, since Jewish records "aren't filed as such."

South Wales's first Jewish community formed in Swansea in the 18th Century, and the Industrial Revolution drew migrants from eastern Europe. Communities thrived in Merthyr Tydfil, Pontypridd and elsewhere, but Merthyr's disappeared by 1999. Project manager Klavdija Erzen attributes the decline partly to success, as children moved away for professional careers, and partly to the collapse of heavy industry. Today Wales has no Jewish schools or kosher shops. If funded, researchers may also create a Cardiff walking trail.

title: Contaminated blood inquiry: Welsh Government urged to take lead
summary:
A lawyer for dozens of contaminated blood scandal victims has urged the Welsh Government to take the lead in helping them. At least 300 people in Wales developed chronic or life-limiting conditions such as hepatitis or HIV after receiving infected blood products in the 1970s and 80s. Across the UK, about 2,400 people died.

Michael Imperato, of Watkins and Gunn, said that although the scandal pre-dates devolution, Wales should now make amends and avoid a "pass the ball" culture. He wants the inquiry to examine the cover-up and how the chain of command worked between the Welsh Office and Whitehall. He asked why the inquiry took 30 to 40 years, saying the establishment ignored victims' pleas. He also criticised the "patchy" and "arbitrary" support available, which forces victims to go "cap in hand" to various organisations.

Health Minister Vaughan Gething said he was committed to supporting victims and would need a good reason not to follow any inquiry recommendations. He promised to keep listening to the affected community. He added that UK nations are discussing a uniform financial support scheme to provide "clarity and parity". The inquiry will hear from Welsh patients and families over four days.

summary:
The US has accused Iran of a "crude and transparent attempt to extort payments from the international community" by breaching the 2015 nuclear deal. European parties created a trade mechanism to bypass US sanctions, but Iran says it is inadequate. Iran's UN representative, Majid Takht-Ravanchi, warned that without action in 60 days, Iran would move to a "third phase."

Iran denies seeking nuclear weapons. Trump wants a broader deal covering Iran's missile programme and regional activities, which Iran has refused.

title: New UK prime minister: Johnson and Hunt await Conservative leadership vote
summary:
Boris Johnson or Jeremy Hunt will be announced as the new Conservative leader, succeeding Theresa May, after a ballot of about 160,000 party members. Mr Johnson, the former London mayor, is the clear favourite. The winner becomes prime minister on Wednesday, after Mrs May chairs her last Prime Minister's Questions and tenders her resignation to the Queen.

Several senior figures have said they won't serve under Mr Johnson. Education Minister Anne Milton resigned just before the result, saying Parliament should play a central role in approving a deal and that the UK must leave the EU responsibly.

Brexit dominated the campaign. Mr Johnson, who led the 2016 Leave campaign, insists the UK must leave on 31 October with or without a deal, and says Mrs May's withdrawal agreement is "dead". Mr Hunt, the foreign secretary, says he is better placed to secure a negotiated exit and would seek more time if needed. Sir Michael Fallon said Mr Johnson would improve the deal in a way Parliament could accept.

The BBC's Nick Eardley said the next PM faces a "daunting in-tray". The EU insists the agreement can't be renegotiated, and many MPs, including some Conservatives, vow to block a no-deal exit.

title: Tory leadership: What's Jeremy Hunt's track record?
summary:
Jeremy Hunt, the Foreign Secretary, will face Boris Johnson in the run-off for Conservative leader and prime minister. He oversaw the London Olympics as culture secretary and was the UK's longest-serving health secretary.

Before entering politics, Hunt taught English in Japan and worked as an entrepreneur. He became MP for South West Surrey in 2005 and served as shadow minister for disabled people, a reward for backing David Cameron, his Oxford contemporary. He became shadow culture secretary in 2007. In 2009, he was ordered to repay over £9,500 after breaching expenses rules by letting his agent stay rent-free in his designated second home, though it was found he hadn't benefited financially.

In 2010, he joined the coalition cabinet as culture, Olympics, media and sport secretary, working closely with then-London Mayor Boris Johnson. He doubled the Olympic ceremonies budget to £81m, and the opening ceremony was widely praised. He pushed for a sporting legacy, but participation rose only modestly, from 34.6% to 36.1% between 2005-06 and 2015-16.

In 2012, his career was threatened when the Leveson Inquiry scrutinised his contacts with News Corp over its BSkyB bid. His special adviser, Adam Smith, resigned.
